summary: Fishing Battery Light, on a man-made island at the Susquehanna River mouth near Havre de Grace, was lit in 1853, moved to a steel tower in 1921, and is closed to visitors.

access.note: Site and tower closed to the public; reachable only by boat (Chesapeake Chapter).

facts.agency: U.S. Department of the Interior (island, since 1942)

events.note: Brick house with integral lantern built by John Donahoo
Station established (USLHS Year Established 1853)
Sixth-order Fresnel lens replaced five lamps with 14-inch reflectors
New lantern replaced the old one, after an 1864 inspection found it defective
Major renovations: new foundation and enlarged building
Bureau of Fisheries bought the island; LighthouseFriends says it had leased it since 1861
Lower floor of the lighthouse removed; keeper's family left with the second floor
A red sector was to be placed in the Fishing Battery station (Cecil Whig)
Keeper William R. Schoenfelder helped save an injured man who had gone overboard from a dredge near the light (October)
Fixed white, oil, changed to flashing white, acetylene; change set for 14 June 1917
Acetylene apparatus installed at a cost of $1,159; LighthouseFriends says this ended the need for a resident keeper
Light moved out of the house lantern to a steel skeleton tower beside the house
Steel skeleton tower, 38 ft (11.6 m); Commissioner's FY1922 report lists $1,545 work completed
Old lantern light discontinued (USLHS Year Discontinued 1921)
Additional red sector approved (Midland Journal)
Keepers lived in the house until 1939 when the light was automated (Chesapeake Chapter); LighthouseFriends gives 1917 instead
Island deeded to the Department of the Interior as part of a migratory bird and wildlife refuge
Hurricane Agnes destroyed what remained of the island's waterfowl vegetation
Wooden parts of the lighthouse torn out and burned as fuel
Metal plaque about the lighthouse's history stolen
Island restored by the Army Corps of Engineers and Fish and Wildlife Service: sand berm, 60,000 plants

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The old lantern light went out when the light moved to the steel tower in 1921 (LighthouseFriends; Chesapeake Chapter; USLHS 'Year Discontinued: 1921'; Commissioner's FY1922 report). The station record's 1925 (Wikidata) is not supported by any source read here.

The Chesapeake Chapter says the light continues to operate as an aid to navigation; the USLHS place record marks it 'Active Aid to Navigation?: No'. The story gives both. The current status was not checked against the Coast Guard Light List.

notes_for_editor: (1) Automation date conflict: LighthouseFriends says the 1917 acetylene apparatus ended the need for a resident keeper, and the roster ends with Schoenfelder in 1917; the Chesapeake Chapter says keepers lived in the house until 1939 when it was automated. Not settled from the records read; the story says so. The 'staffing' field uses 1939 from the Chapter page. (2) Fisheries dates: LighthouseFriends has the Bureau leasing the island from 1861 and buying it in 1891; the 2013 federal report says the island was adapted to a shad hatchery in the mid-1880s. Not reconciled. (3) House description: 1.5 storeys (LighthouseFriends), one storey (Chesapeake Chapter), three storeys (MHT form). Not reconciled. (4) Schoenfelder's first name: Bulletin index 'Robert R.'; Bulletin 1914 text 'William R.' (OCR reads 'Schoenfeider'); FY1915 Commissioner's table 'W. R.'; USLHS roster 'William R.'. The FY1915 entry was matched by its position in the saving-of-life table (printed p. 62, scan 67); check the page image. (5) The current characteristic on the station record (Fl W with two red sectors) was not checked against the Coast Guard Light List; the 1937 newspaper supports the red sectors only. (6) Refuge name: Chapter says Blackwater; LighthouseFriends says Susquehanna Wildlife Refuge; 2013 federal report says Susquehanna National Wildlife Refuge. (7) Not used: Wikipedia (lead only; it gives 1928 for the skeleton tower and 1880-1891 for the Bureau's lease, both contrary to sources used here). The USCG Historian's page could not be read (archived capture 20230927084517 returned no article text; 2024 capture 404). (8) The 1899 Light-House Board entry for 'new model fifth-order lamps' is too garbled by OCR to quote, so it is left out. (9) Newspaper pages were read through newspapers.py. The page-read budget for this station (about 20 reads, including the MHT and NOAA reports) went over the guide's 15. (10) Fact-check pass, 2026-10-28: the 1914, 1917 and index Bulletin PDF page numbers were checked against the cached PDF text (pages 44, 27 and 40). The FY1915 Schoenfelder entry is read from one OCR line, 'W. R. Schoenfelder, keeper, Fishing Battery Light Station, Md.', so the name and station come from the same line; the scanned page image was not opened. The 1914 Bulletin prints the name as 'Schoenfeider' in OCR; the story spells it Schoenfelder, as the USLHS roster and the FY1915 report do. The active-aid disagreement and the conditional 1902 warning are now stated in the story.
